title: Measuring and Reducing Anxious Thoughts and Feelings of Middle Schoolers: An Inner Behavior Intervention
abstract: Abstract The present study investigated the effects of a daily 1-min counting procedure of confident thoughts on self-counted anxious inner behaviors among four middle school students who, following referral by school psychologists, self-identified problematic levels of anxious thoughts and feelings at school. No participant was recruited on the basis of an anxiety diagnosis. Using a multiple baseline design across participants, coupled with pre- and post-intervention interviews, the study systematically evaluated changes in the frequency, celeration, and variability of anxious thoughts and feelings before and during implementation of the intervention. The investigation extends previous inner behavior research by targeting a critical developmental period where anxiety often emerges and can significantly impact academic performance and social development. The pattern and magnitude of change varied across participants. Three participants showed a reversal from accelerating to decelerating anxious thought frequency together with reduced day-to-day variability, and one of the three also showed a substantial reduction in level. The fourth entered the study with an already low and already decelerating frequency and showed no quantitative change that can be attributed to the intervention, though she reported fewer and less severe anxiety attacks. Thematic analysis revealed increased self-awareness, enhanced ability to identify anxiety triggers, and improved emotional regulation strategies. The intervention proved to be feasible, time-efficient, and well-received. The findings support the use of the 1-min counting procedure for confident thoughts as a promising school-based approach for addressing anxiety in adolescents.
